notes.meaning: The psalm opens by praising God before it praises His city. The LORD is great, so He deserves great praise, not ordinary praise. Jerusalem, His 'holy mountain,' was the place He chose to live among His people and be worshiped. Many Christian teachers see it also as a picture of the church, where God is honored above all.

Mount Zion stands high and lovely. It is called 'the joy of all the earth' because there God chose to live with people on a world spoiled by sin. Some teachers see this as a hint that the good news of Jesus would go out from Zion to every nation. 'The city of the great King' means it belongs to God Himself, as Jesus said in Matthew 5:35. Older writers took the line about the north as Zion's place on the city's north side, or as a poetic way to say 'very high.'

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars say Zaphon was a mountain in the far north where the Canaanites thought their gods, including Baal, met. On this view the psalm is saying that Zion, not Zaphon, is the true mountain of God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read 'the sides of the north' as the Gentiles (non-Jewish peoples). Brought out of unbelief, they join Jewish believers on Christ the cornerstone, and the two become one city.

notes.meaning: The city's real safety is not its walls but God Himself. His people know Him as their fortress through long experience. Without God as its defense, no high hill or strong tower could save it.

'Behold' calls us to look at something surprising. Several kings joined forces and marched on Jerusalem, sure that together they would win. We don't know for certain which attack this was. Many think of the enemies who came against King Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20) or the Assyrian army in Hezekiah's day.
The kings came and saw, but they did not conquer. One look at the city was enough. They remembered that God was there to defend it, and they ran in panic. Not one arrow was shot at the city.

Their fear is compared to a woman's labor pains. Those pains are sharp, sudden, and cannot be escaped. It was a common way in that part of the world to describe the worst kind of distress. God can take the courage out of even the proudest enemies of His people.

Ships of Tarshish were the biggest and finest ships of the day. A fierce east wind could smash them in a moment. The point is that God broke these enemies just as quickly and fully. Whether or not real ships were meant, it shows that God rules over every power on earth.

The people had heard stories of what God did in the past and what He promised. Now they have seen the same thing with their own eyes. This makes their faith in God's word stronger. 'Selah' is probably a pause in the song, a moment to stop and think.

differ.view: God would have kept defending Jerusalem in every age, but the city turned away from Him and lost His protection. So the promise depended on staying faithful.
The promise is fully kept in the true church, which is built on Christ the Rock and can never fail.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine says the church heard these things in prophecy and now sees them fulfilled in the gospel. Because God founded the city forever, it will not fall, and he sets its unity against those who split away from it.

notes.meaning: At worship in the temple, the people think deeply about God's 'loving devotion.' That means His faithful, covenant love, the love He has promised to His people. They look back over what He has done before and see His kindness. Every good thing they enjoy flows from His love, not from anything they earned.

God's 'name' means who He is and what He is known for. Wherever people hear of His great deeds, they praise Him, even to the ends of the earth. His 'right hand' stands for His power at work. Everything He does with that power is right and fair.

Jerusalem and 'the daughters of Judah' are called to rejoice. The daughters of Judah are the smaller towns and villages around the city. They are glad because of God's 'judgments.' These are His just actions, here His defeat of the enemies who came against them.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read 'Judah' as meaning 'confession,' so the daughters of Judah are those who confess Christ.

notes.meaning: The people are invited to walk all around the city and count its towers and walls. They find that none was damaged, because God kept the enemy away. They are to remember this and tell their children. Christians have also seen here a picture of the church, made strong by Christ and by God's promises, which we should know well and pass on to the next generation.

The psalm ends by turning our eyes from the walls to God Himself. The God who did all this is our God, and He will be ours forever. He never changes in His love and care. He will guide His people all through life, even to death. Many teachers add that He leads us through death and beyond it, into life with Him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the Hebrew words for 'till death' were really a musical note. They say it probably belongs with the heading of Psalm 49 and was not part of this psalm's last line.
